title: Debugger lab: catch the search race
objective: Choose a breakpoint type for a race bug, pause on the stale response, and read the async call stack to find the cause.
summary: An intro video shows a search box whose late re response overwrites the newer react results and names the Sources panel parts. A stepper lets the learner choose a line-of-code breakpoint, a conditional breakpoint, a logpoint, an XHR/fetch breakpoint or the ignore list and step through the race while the Call Stack and Scope change. A guided walkthrough pauses at each breakpoint type, a deck compares the types, and a summary video connects each bug to its breakpoint.

watch.transcript:
# A search race in the Sources panel

A search box sends a request for re and then for react. The react response arrives first and the late re response renders last, so the list shows the wrong results. The Sources panel has a Navigator, an Editor and a Debugger with the Breakpoints, Scope and Call Stack panes. A breakpoint pauses the page; a logpoint prints to the Console and does not pause.

**00:00 The search box shows the wrong results.** You type react, but the list shows results for re. Why?

**00:06 Two requests race.** The Search box calls onInput twice, for re and then for react. The Server answers react first. The re response comes back late.

**00:17 The Sources panel has three parts.** The Sources panel has three parts. The Navigator lists the files. The Editor shows the code. The Debugger shows Breakpoints, Scope and Call Stack.

**00:28 Breakpoint or logpoint.** A Breakpoint pauses the page, so you can read Scope and the Call Stack. A Logpoint never pauses. It prints a message in the Console.

**00:38 Your plan in this lab.** In this lab you run the race, pause on the stale response, and read the async call stack.

Sources:

- Chrome DevTools documentation: Elements/CSS, Console, JavaScript debugging, Overrides — https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools

scenes.heading: A conditional breakpoint pauses only on the stale response
The ignore list hides library frames

guided.transcript:
# Catching the search race with breakpoints

Line 6 calls render(items) after await search(q). A line breakpoint there pauses twice: first with q react, then with q re, which leaves the wrong list. A conditional breakpoint with q !== input.value pauses only on the stale re response. At that pause the Call Stack shows onInput line 6, an await separator, and onInput line 5 with two vendor frames below. A logpoint prints the same values in the Console without pausing. Adding vendor/events.js to the ignore list hides the two vendor frames.

**00:00 Line 6 calls render(items).** Line 5 waits for search(q). Line 6 calls render(items). We set breakpoints on line 6.

**00:08 A line breakpoint pauses twice.** A line breakpoint on line 6 pauses twice. Pause 1: q is react. Pause 2: q is re, so the list shows re results.

**00:19 A conditional breakpoint pauses only on the stale response.** Now add a condition to line 6: q !== input.value. Condition false means no pause. Condition true pauses on the stale re response.

**00:31 Read the async call stack.** The Call Stack shows onInput app.js:6, then await, then onInput app.js:5. The frames below await show the call that started the wait.

**00:43 A logpoint watches without pausing.** A logpoint on line 6 prints q and input.value. The Console shows render react react, then render re react. The page never pauses.

**00:54 The ignore list hides library frames.** Add vendor/events.js to the ignore list. Ignore list off: five frames. Ignore list on: only your own frames stay in the Call Stack.

Sources:

- Chrome DevTools documentation: Elements/CSS, Console, JavaScript debugging, Overrides — https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools
- ECMA-426: Source map format specification — https://tc39.es/ecma426/
guided.explanation: The async part of the Call Stack, below the await separator, shows the call that started the wait. Its Scope still holds the old q, so you see that a stale response reached render.

A conditional breakpoint with q !== input.value pauses only on the stale re response. At that pause the Call Stack shows onInput line 6, an await separator, and onInput line 5 with two vendor frames below. A logpoint prints the same values in the Console without pausing. Adding vendor/events.js to the ignore list hides the two vendor frames.

summary_video.transcript:
# Pick the breakpoint for the bug

Use a line-of-code breakpoint when you know the line, a conditional breakpoint when only some calls are wrong, and a logpoint when you must not pause. When you do not know the line, break on the cause: an XHR or fetch request, a DOM change, an event listener or an exception. At the pause read Scope and the Call Stack; async frames show who started the wait and the ignore list hides library frames. The search race is fixed by returning early when q !== input.value.

**00:00 Pick the breakpoint for the bug.** Which breakpoint catches which bug?

**00:05 When you know the line.** Know the line? Use a line-of-code breakpoint. Only some calls are wrong? Use a conditional breakpoint. Must not pause? Use a logpoint.

**00:16 When you do not know the line.** When you do not know the line, break on the cause: a fetch request, a DOM change, an event listener, or an exception.

**00:27 Read the pause.** At the pause, read Scope for the values and the Call Stack for the callers. Async frames show who started the wait. The ignore list hides library frames.

**00:39 Fix the race.** The bug: render used a stale response. The fix on line 6: return when q !== input.value.

Sources:

- Chrome DevTools documentation: Elements/CSS, Console, JavaScript debugging, Overrides — https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools

Log or pause on a condition

deck.outline:
# Which breakpoint type fits this bug

A short deck about choosing a breakpoint type. The main path splits bugs into those where you know the line and those where you do not, then shows what to read at the pause. Two deep dives compare a logpoint with a conditional breakpoint and list the three DOM change breakpoint types.

**Purpose.** Choose a breakpoint type from the symptom of a bug: known line, only some calls, no pause allowed, or an unknown line.

## Main path

### 1. Which breakpoint finds this bug?

**On screen.** Title card with "Start from what you know".

**Notes.** Ask the learner what they know about the bug before they choose a breakpoint type.

### 2. You know the line

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: Every call: line-of-code breakpoint → Only some calls: conditional breakpoint → No pause allowed: logpoint.

**Notes.** Reveal each case. The three types all sit on one line of code and differ in when they stop.

**Branches.** deep dive "Logpoint or conditional breakpoint".

### 3. You do not know the line

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: A request: XHR/fetch breakpoint → A changed node: DOM change breakpoint → A click or key: event listener breakpoint → A thrown error: exception breakpoint.

**Notes.** When the line is unknown, pause on the cause: a request, a DOM change, an event or an exception.

**Branches.** deep dive "DOM change breakpoint types".

### 4. Then read the pause

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: Scope: the values now → Call Stack: who called → Async frames: who started the wait.

**Notes.** At every pause, read Scope for the values and the Call Stack, including the async frames, for the callers.

### 5. Choose the closest pause

**On screen.** Two columns, "Line known" and "Line unknown", fill in pairs; verdict: Pause where the cause happens..

**Notes.** The best breakpoint stops closest to the cause, so you read the state before it changes again.

## Deep dive: Logpoint or conditional breakpoint

### 1. Log or pause on a condition

**On screen.** Two columns, "Conditional breakpoint" and "Logpoint", fill in pairs; verdict: Log when pausing changes the timing..

**Notes.** A conditional breakpoint pauses only when its expression is true; a logpoint never pauses and prints its message in the Console.

## Deep dive: DOM change breakpoint types

### 1. Three DOM change breakpoints

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: Subtree modifications: a child changes → Attribute modifications: an attribute changes → Node removal: the node is removed.

**Notes.** In the Elements panel you choose which change pauses: a child changes, an attribute changes, or the node is removed.
deck.explanation: A breakpoint type is a question you ask the browser: pause on this line, pause only when this is true, log without pausing, or pause when this event, request or DOM change happens.

checkpoints.prompt: You set a line-of-code breakpoint on line 6 and run the race: re, then react. How often does it pause, and what is q at the last pause?

choices.text: Twice; q is re at the last pause

choices.misconception: Thinks a line breakpoint pauses only on the first or the latest call

choices.text: Twice; q is react at the last pause
choices.misconception: Thinks responses always arrive in the order the requests were sent

checkpoints.explanation: A line-of-code breakpoint pauses every time line 6 runs. Each response runs line 6 once, and the slow re response arrives last, so the last pause has q re and render then shows stale results.

checkpoints.prompt: In the stepper, choose the breakpoint type that pauses only on the stale response, and step until it pauses with q re while the input says react.

goal.hint: Load the conditional breakpoint preset and press Forward until the condition shows true.

checkpoints.explanation: A conditional breakpoint pauses only when its expression is true. q !== input.value is true only for the late re response, so the one pause lands on the bug.

checkpoints.prompt: At the pause, the Call Stack shows onInput app.js:6, then await, then onInput app.js:5. What do the frames below await tell you?

choices.text: Which call started the wait that has now resumed
Functions that run after render returns
choices.misconception: Thinks the Call Stack lists future calls instead of past callers

choices.text: A second thread that runs onInput at the same time
choices.misconception: Thinks await runs code in parallel on another thread

checkpoints.explanation: The async call stack keeps the stack from the moment the code started waiting. The frames below await show the onInput call on line 5 that sent this request.

checkpoints.prompt: Pausing changes the timing, and the race disappears. Which type shows q at line 6 on every call?

choices.misconception: Thinks a conditional breakpoint logs instead of pausing when true
Thinks a fetch breakpoint pauses when the response arrives

checkpoints.explanation: A logpoint prints its message in the Console each time the line runs and never pauses, so the order of the two responses stays the same.

checkpoints.prompt: You add vendor/events.js to the ignore list. What changes at the next pause?

choices.text: The vendor frames disappear from the Call Stack; your frames stay

choices.misconception: Thinks ignore listing disables the script instead of hiding its frames

choices.text: The await separator and the async frames disappear
choices.misconception: Thinks ignore listing removes the async part of the stack

checkpoints.explanation: Ignore listing is a debugging view setting. The library still runs, but its frames are hidden from the Call Stack and stepping skips them, so you see only your own code.

checkpoints.prompt: Something empties a list on the page and you do not know which script does it. Which breakpoint do you set?

choices.text: A DOM change breakpoint (subtree modifications) on the list

choices.misconception: Thinks you must know the line before you can pause

choices.text: A logpoint on the list element
choices.misconception: Thinks logpoints attach to DOM nodes instead of lines of code

checkpoints.explanation: A DOM change breakpoint pauses on the code that changes the node, so the Call Stack then shows the unknown script and line.

checkpoints.prompt: In one or two sentences: how did the conditional pause and the async call stack lead you to the fix?
checkpoints.explanation: The pause showed q re while the input said react, and the frames below await showed it came from the older onInput call. So render must return early when q !== input.value.
